documents.title: NAFTNet Standards for Fetal Treatment Centers

chunks.content: 1 Introduction Congenital diaphragmatic hernia (CDH) is a severe anomaly characterised by a defect in the diaphragm that allows abdominal organs to herniate into the thoracic cavity, impairing normal lung development [ ]. Assessment of Foetal lung size to estimate severity of pulmonary hypoplasia is crucial for prenatal risk stratification, selection for Foetal intervention and delivery planning, as pulmonary hypoplasia along with pulmonary hypertension remain the primary determinants of neonatal mortality and morbidity in CDH [ , , , , ]. Recent multicenter data also confirm that prenatal imaging markers retain prognostic value even in very preterm infants with CDH ≤ 32 weeks, where pulmonary hypoplasia remains a dominant determinant of survival despite the additive morbidity of prematurity [ ]. Ultrasound (US) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) are the primary imaging modalities used to evaluate pulmonary hypoplasia prenatally [ , , , , , ]. On US, the observed‐to‐expected lung‐to‐head ratio (o/e LHR) is a widely accepted metric for estimating pulmonary hypoplasia [ ] and has been shown to correlate with neonatal mortality [ , , , ] and morbidity [ , ]. Although simple in theory to obtain, there is a significant learning curve with at least 70 measurements to be performed to reach competency [ ]. Furthermore, reproducibility varies depending on lung area measurement method used [ , , ] and varies across Foetal medicine centers depending on the center size and experience [ , ]. As MRI is less limited by technical factors and provides excellent contrast between lung and surrounding structures, it is increasingly utilized in addition to US to refine antenatal prognostication. MRI allows for the assessment of the total Foetal lung volume (TFLV) in three dimensions to generate the o/e TFLV, which is a significant predictor of mortality [ , , , , ]. Although single center studies have demonstrated good reproducibility in Foetal lung volume assessment by MRI [ , , , , ], more recently, a large multicenter collaboration across the North American Foetal Therapy Network demonstrated significant heterogeneity between reviewers for Foetal lung volume estimations [ ]. This variability in lung size estimations may largely be due to lack of standardisation of imaging protocols [ , ], but additionally suboptimal imaging conditions due to Foetal or maternal factors, limiting accurate measurement. Furthermore, we have recently demonstrated discrepancies between US and MRI lung volume assessments, particularly in cases of non‐severe left CDH on US (i.e., o/e LHR > 25%). In approximately one third of these cases, MRI measurements of Foetal lung volume were consistent with severe left CDH and correlated better with actual neonatal outcomes [ ]. Given this discrepancy and the limitations of quantitative measures, there may be a role for qualitative impressions of Foetal lung size to help estimate CDH severity, especially when quantitative metrics are straddling the severity thresholds and/or measurement condition and image quality are suboptimal. Additionally, qualitative assessment may be useful in cases where counselling is conducted virtually after remote image review, particularly when measurements are not available. Thus, the aim of our study was to evaluate the reproducibility and correlation of qualitative assessments of Foetal lung size on US and MRI with quantitative metrics including o/e LHR and o/e TFLV respectively in left CDH. Additionally, we sought to assess the correlation between these qualitative assessments and neonatal mortality during initial hospitalisation after birth in infants with CDH. 2 Methods This was a retrospective study of foetuses referred with prenatally diagnosed CDH to the Ontario Foetal Centre, Toronto, Canada, between January 2008 and December 2020. The Ontario Foetal Centre is a collaboration between Mount Sinai Hospital and The Hospital for Sick Children in Toronto and serves as a tertiary referral center. Ethical approval for this study was granted by both hospital institutional review boards (REB #13‐0077‐C and 1000006184). Foetuses with prenatally detected right CDH or bilateral CDH, additional genetic or structural anomalies and cases of Foetal intervention with Foetal endoscopic tracheal occlusion (FETO) and postnatal palliation were excluded. This ensures a homogeneous cohort in which outcomes reflect the severity of CDH rather than external management factors or non–CDH‐related pathology. US images were obtained using GE Voluson E10 (GE Healthcare, Zipf, Austria) or Philips IU22 (Philips, Amsterdam, The Netherlands) US machines. Digitally stored US images were reviewed independently by two experienced Foetal medicine specialists (N.A., S.S., each with 8 and 5 years of experience, respectively) who were blinded to the neonatal outcome. Both reviewers together retrospectively reviewed US images obtained at the time of initial referral, generally within 2–3 weeks of MRI. Digitally stored US images were reviewed independently by two experienced Foetal medicine specialists (N.A., S.S., each with 8 and 5 years of experience, respectively) who were blinded to the neonatal outcome. Both reviewers together retrospectively reviewed US images obtained at the time of initial referral, generally within 2–3 weeks of MRI. The highest‐quality image of the Foetal chest was selected, on which a lung area would typically be measured for o/e LHR determination as per our imaging protocols for CDH prognostication [ ]. Specifically, a transverse section of the chest with a four‐chamber view of the heart with the right lung as close as possible to the transducer [ ], was assessed independently by each reviewer and categorised into mild, moderate or severe pulmonary hypoplasia based on qualitative assessment of lung size (i.e., visual inspection alone) and presence or absence of intrathoracic liver herniation. Based on our experience in assessing o/e LHR over many years, the severity of pulmonary hypoplasia was estimated visually as mild, moderate or severe by evaluating: (1) apparent lung volume/degree of compression, (2) degree of mediastinal shift and cardiac compression, and (3) presence of liver herniation, assessed by direct visualisation of liver within the thorax and stomach position (Figure ). The quantitative measurement of the lung area, obtained by the same reviewers more than a year prior to the qualitative assessment [ ], was done utilising the ‘trace method’, owing to its higher inter‐rater agreement compared with other methods [ , ]. The o/e LHR was determined using the calculator provided by the Tracheal Occlusion To Accelerate Lung Growth trial ( www.totaltrial.eu ). Severity of CDH was based on o/e‐LHR and the presence of liver herniation, consistent with previously described algorithms for the prediction of survival in LCDH [ , ]. Specifically, an o/e‐LHR of ≤ 25.0% was defined as severe pulmonary hypoplasia; an o/e‐LHR of 25.1%–34.9% irrespective of liver position or 35.0%–44.9% with liver herniation was considered moderate hypoplasia; and an o/e‐LHR of ≥ 45.0% irrespective of liver position or 35.0%–44.9% without liver herniation was defined as mild hypoplasia. Foetal MRI images were reviewed retrospectively by two experienced Foetal medicine radiologists (D.K. and S.J, each with 10 and 9 years of experience, respectively) who were blinded to the neonatal outcome. MRI studies were obtained in conjunction with US as part of comprehensive antenatal risk stratification. MRI studies were performed on a 1.5 T magnet (GE Signa; GE Healthcare, Waukesha, WI) as per the institutional Foetal lung protocol and included triplane T2‐weighted single shot fast spin echo (SSFSE) sequences with contiguously acquired slices at a thickness of 3–5 mm, in addition to the routinely acquired True Fast Imaging with Steady‐State Free Precession (TRUFI) and T1 images. Both reviewers independently reviewed all studies and qualitatively estimated Foetal lung size by visual inspection alone and classified each case as either severe or non‐ severe (Figure ). Subjective assessment of lung volume into severe (TFLV < 35%) and non‐severe (TFLV ≥ 35%) categories was based on both reviewers' extensive experience interpreting high‐volume Foetal MRI over many years. Multiplanar assessment was particularly valuable. Severe cases were defined by near‐complete replacement of the ipsilateral lung by herniated abdominal contents with associated mediastinal shift and contralateral lung compression. These impressions were supported on T1‐weighted imaging by the presence of significant liver herniation and meconium at the ipsilateral lung apex, indicating markedly limited residual lung tissue. Conversely, non‐severe cases demonstrated preserved ipsilateral lung volume, visible contralateral lung tissue without significant mediastinal displacement, absent or minimal liver herniation, and no bowel loops at the lung apex (FIgure ). The o/e TFLV was subsequently measured for each study by both radiologists independently and categorised as severe (i.e., o/e TFLV ≤ 35%) or non‐severe (if o/e‐> 35%) based on our institutional data which has demonstrated a survival rate of 20% in foetuses with o/e TFLV ≤ 35% [ ]. All US and MRI assessments, both qualitative and quantitative were correlated with neonatal mortality in infants with left CDH during initial hospitalisation following birth. Multivariate analysis was not performed because perinatal factors such as liver position, gestational age at delivery, and Foetal size add limited incremental predictive value once imaging findings are accounted for [ ], and because our primary objective was to assess whether subjective assessment could approximate objective measurement. 3 Statistics Descriptive statistics, including medians and inter‐quartile ranges (IQR), were calculated to analyse the data. The association between reviewers' qualitative assessments of Foetal lung size and the quantitative measurements of o/e LHR and o/e TFLV by US and MRI respectively was assessed using weighted Kappa for US assessments as is done for multi‐class variables and Cohen's Kappa statistics for MRI evaluation as is done for binary variables. Accordingly, the degree of agreement was evaluated as “none” to “slight” if the coefficient was 0–0.2, “fair” if 0.21–0.4, “moderate” if 0.41–0.6, “substantial” if 0.61–0.8, and “almost perfect” if 0.81–1 [ , ]. The association between the qualitative assessment of Foetal lung size and mortality outcome (within initial hospitalisation after birth) was investigated using the Chi‐square test. Spearman's correlation was used to assess the strength of the association between o/e LHR and mortality prior to discharge from hospital, with correlations of 0.01–0.19 considered “very weak”, 0.20–0.39 “weak”, 0.40–0.59 “moderate”, 0.60–0.79 “strong”, and 0.80–1.00 “very strong”. The strength of the association between o/e TFLV and CDH mortality during initial hospitalisation was measured using Cramér's V, where values of 0–0.1 were considered “negligible”, 0.1–0.2 “weak”, 0.2–0.4 “moderate”, 0.4–0.6 “relatively strong”, 0.6–0.8 “strong” and 0.8–1.0 “very strong”. SAS software (version 9.4, SAS Institute Inc., Cary, NC) was used for statistical analysis. 4 Results During this 13‐year study period, 253 pregnancies with CDH were referred to the Ontario Foetal Centre for assessment. After excluding pregnancy terminations ( n = 75), infants with palliative care postnatally ( n = 15) and right or bilateral CDH ( n = 22), 141 infants with left CDH which underwent active perinatal care remained for analysis. Cases with additional genetic or structural anomalies ( n = 25), as well as foetuses which had FETO ( n = 13) were also excluded. Of the remaining 103 cases, 74 underwent both prenatal US and MRI and comprised our study cohort (Figure ). Left CDH was diagnosed at a median GA of 22.4 (IQR 20.4–29.4) weeks. US images reviewed for qualitative Foetal lung size assessment and o/e LHR determination were performed at a median GA of 24.4 (IQR 22.1–31.2) weeks. MRI was performed at a median GA of 27.0 (IQR 26.0–29.4) weeks. The median interval between US and MRI assessments was 2.86 (IQR 1.29–5.29) weeks. US determined o/e LHR demonstrated a moderate correlation with neonatal mortality during initial hospitalisation (o/e LHR: Spearman's Correlation −0.49, p < 0.0001), while MRI measured o/e TFLV demonstrated a relatively strong correlation with neonatal mortality during initial hospitalisation (o/e TFLV: Cramér's V correlation of 0.44, p = 0.0002). 4.1 Assessment of Pulmonary Hypoplasia 4.1.1 Qualitative Fetal Lung Size Assessment by US Inter‐rater agreement for qualitative assessment of Foetal lung size by both reviewers (S.S. and N.A.) was strong with the weighted Kappa coefficient of 0.80 (95% CI 0.68, 0.93) (Figure ). Strong agreement was also noted for the qualitative Foetal lung size assessment and the measured o/e LHR for each reviewer separately (Reviewer 1: weighted Kappa 0.67 (95% CI 0.52, 0.81) and Reviewer 2: weighted Kappa 0.68 (95% CI 0.55, 0.82)) (Figure ). Similarly to quantitatively measured o/e LHR, qualitative assessments of Foetal lung size demonstrated a moderate correlation with neonatal mortality during initial hospitalisation in foetuses with left CDH (Spearman's correlation: −0.44, p < 0.0001) for Reviewer 1, and 0.43, p < 0.0001 for Reviewer 2 (Figures and ). 4.1.2 Qualitative Foetal Lung Size Assessment by MRI When comparing qualitative assessment of Foetal lung size by MRI, inter‐rater agreement between both reviewers (D.K. and S.J.) was moderate (Cohen's Kappa coefficient of 0.48 (95% CI 0.30, 0.66)). Correlation was strong between the qualitative assessment of Foetal lung size with measured o/e TFLV (Reviewer 1: Cohen's Kappa 0.69, 95% CI 0.5231, 0.8550 and Reviewer 2: Cohen's Kappa 0.61 (95% CI 0.4294, 0.7911, Figure )). Similar to US, qualitative assessments of Foetal lung size by MRI demonstrated a moderate correlation with neonatal mortality prior to discharge in foetuses with left CDH (Reviewer 1: Cramér's 0.34 ( p = 0.004), Reviewer 2: Cramér's V 0.35 ( p = 0.002), Figures and ). 5 Discussion 5.1 Principal Findings In this study, we highlight the utility of qualitative assessments of Foetal lung size in the prenatal evaluation of isolated left CDH by US and MRI, focusing on the agreement between reviewers and the correlation between qualitative assessments with quantitative measurements of lung size commonly used in clinical practice for neonatal mortality prediction. Principal Findings In this study, we highlight the utility of qualitative assessments of Foetal lung size in the prenatal evaluation of isolated left CDH by US and MRI, focusing on the agreement between reviewers and the correlation between qualitative assessments with quantitative measurements of lung size commonly used in clinical practice for neonatal mortality prediction. When assessing Foetal lung size qualitatively, interrater agreement was strong by US and moderate by MRI. When comparing qualitative assessments of Foetal lung size to quantitative measurements (i.e., o/e LHR by US and o/e TFLV by MRI), the agreement was similarly strong for US and MRI. While qualitative and quantitative sonographic assessments of Foetal lung size correlated similarly with neonatal mortality prior to discharge during initial hospitalisation in infants with left CDH, quantitative measurements by MRI demonstrated a greater correlation with CDH mortality during the initial hospitalisation when compared to qualitative assessments. 5.2 Strengths and Limitations To the best of our knowledge, qualitative assessment of Foetal lung size and its reproducibility in the prediction of mortality associated with left CDH has not been previously studied. This study, however, is not without limitations. First, our retrospective, single‐centre design limits external validity and introduces potential selection bias. Of all left CDH cases meeting inclusion criteria, only 74 had both US and MRI. This attrition could bias the sample toward patients with more complete imaging or different disease severity. Second, the reliance on expert reviewers from a tertiary/quaternary Foetal medicine centre with expertise in CDH limits the generalizability of these findings to less experienced practitioners and centres and thus, should not be used in isolation for prognostication when counselling parents prenatally, or when deciding on candidacy for Foetal therapy. Nonetheless, qualitative lung assessment could be standardised using predefined image criteria (such as evaluation of lung compression, mediastinal shift and echogenicity patterns to distinguish lung, liver and bowel), exemplar teaching sets covering the full severity spectrum, and structured reporting templates. This may assist with improving reproducibility of qualitative assessments outside of tertiary centres. Additionally, the 2.8‐week interval between US and MRI may allow for lung growth or a change in disease severity, potentially affecting inter‐modality comparisons. Nonetheless, since o/e LHR and o/e TFLV are theoretically GA independent, this interval likely had little impact on comparisons. Moreover, while neonatal death was chosen as the primary outcome, other outcomes such as the need for extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) or long‐term respiratory morbidity were not explored, which could provide a more comprehensive understanding of the clinical utility of qualitative assessment of lung size. Finally, variability in imaging quality and Foetal positioning may have influenced the strength of the correlations observed, for both US and MRI. 5.3 Interpretation The observed strong agreement between both reviewers for qualitative assessment of Foetal lung size by US underscores its reliability as a practical and widely accessible tool. This consistency is particularly valuable in clinical settings, where US is often the first‐line modality and, at times, the only modality available for prenatal diagnosis and counselling. In contrast to US, we found moderate agreement between reviewers for MRI‐based qualitative lung volume assessment. This may reflect challenges inherent to this modality. While MRI offers superior volumetric accuracy, the technical challenge of delineating liver and mediastinal boundaries on MRI, particularly in the absence of a diaphragm, and the similar signal intensities of liver and adjacent viscera, may make accurate segmentation operator‐dependent [ ]. Moreover, qualitative interpretation of static images might be less intuitive compared to real‐time US. Variability in MRI sequences, Foetal positioning, and a steeper learning curve for interpreting subtle findings may additionally contribute to this moderate concordance between reviewers. These findings are consistent with our recent multicentre study evaluating the reproducibility of antenatal CDH prognosticators by MRI, which demonstrated noticeable variability in o/e TFLV and liver herniation assessment by MRI across the North American Foetal Therapy Network (NAFTNet). This emphasises the need for standardisation of MRI protocols for CDH prognostication to ensure reliable and reproducible Foetal risk stratification. Notably, we found substantial agreement between qualitative assessments of Foetal lung size and the measured o/e LHR on US and o/e TFLV on MRI. This correlation suggests that qualitative assessments can approximate quantitative prognostic indicators of pulmonary hypoplasia. Of particular clinical significance is the finding of a relatively strong correlation between qualitative Foetal lung size estimation and neonatal mortality on US and MRI. Although quantitative metrics, such as o/e LHR and o/e TFLV, are essential in ensuring standardised prognostication for parental counselling, Foetal therapy considerations and in research settings, qualitative assessments may still offer a complementary perspective, particularly in cases where quantitative measures are borderline or difficult to obtain. The ability of qualitative assessment to predict neonatal outcome, reinforces their role in holistic risk stratification. Although quantitative metrics, such as o/e LHR and o/e TFLV, are essential in ensuring standardised prognostication for parental counselling, Foetal therapy considerations and in research settings, qualitative assessments may still offer a complementary perspective, particularly in cases where quantitative measures are borderline or difficult to obtain. The ability of qualitative assessment to predict neonatal outcome, reinforces their role in holistic risk stratification. Additionally, combining qualitative impressions with quantitative techniques, such as machine learning algorithms for automated volume estimation, could further refine prenatal prognostication in CDH. Such attempts have recently been made using automatic lung and liver MRI segmentation in CDH [ ]. 6 Conclusion In conclusion, this study demonstrates that qualitative estimation of Foetal lung size, by US more so than MRI, is reproducible and clinically meaningful in the prenatal evaluation of left CDH, and correlates with quantitative measures. The association of these assessments with neonatal mortality underscores their potential role in risk stratification and counselling. Nonetheless, quantitative measurements of Foetal lung size for risk stratification and candidacy for FETO should remain the gold standard in Foetal evaluation. Future research should focus on exploring the integration of qualitative and quantitative measurements of Foetal lung size to optimise prenatal prognostication, counselling and care for foetuses with CDH.
